Full entity stack — how the three layers connect
WaterCo (SPV)
Private operating company. Sells water to commercial/industrial clients. 15% of net distributable profits are contractually and constitutionally obligated to flow to the Trust. No government off-taker.
Community Prosperity Water Trust
Receives 15% annual profit share. Distributes via two-tier formula to all registered QCOs. Governed by an elected board drawn from QCO representatives. Master of the High Court oversight.
Qualifying Community Organisations (QCOs)
Independent, apolitical, geography-based groups: sports clubs, ratepayers associations, neighbourhood watch, SGBs, faith outreach, old age committees, garden cooperatives. Each has its own bank account with 3+ signatories.
Golden share holder
Reputable civic or legal entity (e.g. NMBM Chamber, independent law firm) holding veto rights over any amendment to the 15% clause in WaterCo's MOI. This is the constitutional lock — no single founder or investor can undo it.
Two-tier distribution — equal floor, needs-based bridge
Tier 1 — the equal dividend
The ground floor · pure mathematics
50%
50% of Trust annual income is divided absolutely equally among all registered QCOs. If there are 60 groups, each gets 1/60th. A sports club in Summerstrand gets the same base grant as a soup kitchen in Zwide. This is collective prosperity: the formula is mathematics, not politics. It is impossible to manipulate because there are no criteria — only the headcount of registered QCOs.
One group · one equal shareFunds basic operating costs or member-decided projects
Tier 2 — the bridging project fund
Scaled infrastructure · needs-based
50%
50% goes into a project fund. QCOs apply with proposals. The Trust board — elected from QCO representatives — scores applications against a transparent criteria matrix. Larger infrastructure allocations flow to highest-need areas first, rapidly closing the divide.

Qualifying community organisation formation — bootstrapping civil society
What qualifies as a QCO
Any formally constituted, apolitical, geography-based group within the NMBM boundary. Minimum 5 members. Own bank account. Simple one-page constitution. Annual elected committee.

The three pilot suburbs

Formation process — remove every bureaucratic hurdle
01
Community Water Ambassadors
Hire 2–3 young people from target suburbs, paid a modest stipend. Their mandate: go group to group, explain the Trust, say "form a 5-person committee, open a bank account, adopt our one-page constitution — and you will receive an equal annual share of water profits, forever."
02
Free formation kit
Provide a ready-made one-page constitution template and free bank account setup support via a local credit union or digital bank (TymeBank, Capitec). Remove every reason to say it is too hard.
03
R1,000 inception grant on registration
Once a group formally registers and opens an account, the Trust issues a R1,000 inception grant automatically. This is the first tangible proof that the system is not politics — it is real money in their account, conditioned on nothing but their own self-organisation.
04
One suburb, one voice — the community forum
Longer-term target: each recognised suburb or ward has a unified "Community Forum" that selects one representative to the Trust's beneficiary assembly. Start by recognising all existing groups immediately so money flows from day one — consolidate the forum model over 12–18 months.
Funding the formation — your cost, not the community's
Ambassador stipends, formation kit, and inception grants are funded by WaterCo's corporate social investment or marketing budget — not from the 15% profit share. This is your cost of building a social licence. It is cheaper than any legal battle against a community protest.
Inoculation against criminal-political capture — design features
Three-signatory bank accounts — no single gatekeeper
Every QCO's grant is paid directly into its own bank account requiring a minimum of three unrelated signatories (chairperson, treasurer, secretary), all residents of that suburb, all elected annually. No single person controls any community's funds.
Rotating representation — no professional trustee kingpins
Trust board members serve 2-year terms with a mandatory 1-term cooling-off period before re-election. This structurally prevents the emergence of entrenched power over the distribution process.
Radical digital transparency — public quarterly reporting
All Trust income, distributions, and project decisions are published on a public website updated quarterly. Any community member with a phone can see exactly what their group received and what every other group received. Transparency is the disinfectant.
Independent annual audit — posted publicly
Books audited annually by a reputable, non-politically-connected mid-tier firm. Audit report posted on the public website. Any material finding triggers automatic notification to the Master of the High Court.
Third-party whistle-blower hotline
A small portion of Trust operating budget funds a confidential, third-party-run hotline for community members to report attempted corruption or intimidation within any QCO or the Trust board. Anonymity guaranteed, managed externally.
Distributed network — impractical to capture
When funds flow equally to 50+ independent groups each with their own bank account and elected committee, there is no single point to corrupt. To capture the income stream, a syndicate would have to infiltrate 50 different clubs simultaneously — operationally and socially impossible.
International arbitration for all major contracts
All WaterCo customer contracts and investor agreements include international arbitration clauses. This places commercial dispute resolution entirely outside local political jurisdiction — a powerful deterrent against state-adjacent interference.

Immediate execution — this week through month 3
W1
Instruct your attorney: Trust Deed + MOI amendment
Draft the Trust Deed with the two-tier distribution model, the irrevocable MOI link, and the golden share structure. Simultaneously draft the one-page QCO constitution template. These two documents are the legal DNA of the entire venture.
W2
Identify the first two pilot QCOs
One existing sports club (Lorraine/Sunridge profile), one church or community group (Motherwell/KwaNobuhle profile). Offer to help them complete the simple QCO registration. Tell them they will be the first beneficiaries when the Trust receives its first profit distribution.
M1
Hire Community Water Ambassadors
Two young people, one from a historically white suburb, one from a township — paid a monthly stipend funded by WaterCo's CSI budget. Their mandate: map every existing group in their network and begin the QCO registration process using the formation kit.
M2
Embed the Trust in your investor pitch
Tell impact investors: "We have eliminated political and community expropriation risk by embedding the local population as direct financial beneficiaries. Our social licence is built into our share register." The 15% is not a cost — it is your primary risk mitigation instrument and your competitive moat.
M3
Launch the public transparency dashboard
Even before the first distribution, publish the Trust Deed, the QCO register, and the distribution formula publicly. This pre-empts any narrative of secrecy and makes the model visible to every ward councillor, journalist, and community member before any money moves.
The complete positioning statement
You are not a privatiser. You are a community-rooted, profit-sharing utility.
You do what the municipality cannot: deliver reliable water to business, and in doing so, build a perpetual, self-funding source of community prosperity across every suburb of Gqeberha. The trust is not your philanthropy — it is your architecture.
